catalog_quote: Ede Chaabe [èdèē tʃáàbɛ́] is an Eastern Ede language of the Benue-Congo family spoken in the Central and South-Central part of Benin, with Savè representing the district with the largest number of Ede Chaabe speakers (87,177 people, according to the 2013 RGPH4 census). It is a language with three lexical level tones, L, M, and H, as shown in the minimal triplet in (1). ... (1) Three tone levels a. kí ‘greet’ b. kī ‘set fire/burn’ c. kì ‘praise/recite one’s panegyric’ Just like its better studied sister language Yoruba, Ede Chaabe contrasts three lexical tones and shares some of the word-level tonal constraints and processes found in Yoruba, including a tonotactic constraint against H tones on the initial vowel of vowel-initial words (e.g. VCV, VCVCV).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ede Cabe/Chaabe is a register-tone language with three contrastive level tones (L, M, H) on every syllable/vowel (minimal triplet kí 'greet', kī 'burn', kì 'praise'); the accessible modern descriptions (Mamadou 2023, 2025) describe word-level tone and sentence intonation only and make no statement about word stress or accent. The one work that explicitly treats 'accent' (stress) and its interaction with tone and intonation is Alo (1991), a Lyon 2 thesis with no online full text.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tonal notes: no H tone on the initial vowel of vowel-initial words; V1/M-tone deletion in hiatus; H-tone contour formation from the resumptive subject pronoun; question intonation adds a L% boundary tone with extended lowering (Mamadou 2023: 100-104; 2025: 86-87).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone at word level; intonation discussed at utterance level (statements, yes/no questions, exclamations). Data from native speakers of Savè and Tchaourou (Mamadou 2023: 105); author is a native speaker.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources use the names Ede Chaabe (Mamadou 2023, 2025; ISO cbj given explicitly), Caabe (Mamadou Yacoubou et al. 2020), Cabé/Cabɛ (Alo 1991, Idohou 2009), Tsabe (Akinkugbe 1978) and Cabe (Kluge 2011); all refer to the Savè-Tchaourou variety of Benin = Glottolog edec1238. Kluge 2011 Vol. 1 distinguishes Cabe (Savè) and Cabe (Tchaourou) sub-varieties; Mamadou's speakers come from both towns.

sources.note: Section 3 'Background on Ede Chaabe' (p. 86) states the language has three lexical level tones L, M, H (minimal triplet ki), shares Yoruba word-level tonal constraints (no H on initial vowel of V-initial words), and describes vowel/tone deletion; the words 'stress'/'accent' never occur in reference to Chaabe. Sentence prosody (yes/no question L% boundary tone and extended lowering) is treated in sections 4-6.

sources.citation: Mamadou Yacoubou, Tajudeen. 2023. Tone and intonation modeling in African tone languages. PhD dissertation, Rutgers University. DOI 10.7282/t3-azyy-3728. 179 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Section 5.1-5.1.1 (pp. 100-104) gives the Chaabe background and surface tonology: 'Ede Chaabe contrasts three lexical tones.. H, M and L' (p. 101), contour formation, V1/M deletion; nothing on stress in Chaabe. Only generic remark (p. 53) that tone languages lack 'lexically stressed syllables or phrasal pitch accent', motivating a model not based on metrical strength. Quotes Alo (1991:114) on question-final pitch lowering.
